items.title: anxious, typo'd, night before
turns: i have a interveiw tomorow and im so nervous i cant sleep, what do i do
replies:
Deep breath — you can calm this. Quick, practical plan to sleep and be sharp tomorrow.
1) Tonight — get rest fast
- Put your phone away now (no screens) or use Do Not Disturb. Blue light and notifications keep you wired.
- Do a 10–15 minute “pre-mortem” journaling: write the worst-case interview scenario, then one line next to each saying how you’d handle it. This clears panic.
- Do a 7–10 minute guided breathing: 4s inhale, 6s exhale, repeat. Lie down and do it until you feel calmer.
- If your mind races, do a short checklist: outfit picked, resume printed/accessible, interview link/phone charged, water, directions/time zone. Once checked, close it — you handled it.
- Use a sleep aid only if you already use it (melatonin 1–3 mg, or whatever your normal). Don’t try new meds.
- If you’re still awake after 30 minutes, get up, read a low-stakes paper book under a dim light for 15 minutes, then try again.
2) One-hour prep before bed (or in morning if you prefer)
- Review the job description for 10 minutes and pick 3 key things they want.
- Pick 3 stories from your past that show impact: problem, action, result. Make each 1–2 minutes. From what I know: use your Copperline Infra intern story (Python service that cut reporting from 2 hours to 15 minutes), your Treasurer role (managed $4,000 budget), and one school project or class team [fill in if you want].
- Write a 30–45 second “why me” pitch: who you are (student, major), top skill, one achievement, and why you want this role at their company. Practice it twice out loud.
3) Morning-of checklist (30–45 minutes before)
- Eat a light protein-rich breakfast, hydrate.
- Do a 5-minute vocal warm-up (read your pitch out loud, smile while speaking).
- Review your 3 stories and job description one last time.
- Test tech: camera, mic, internet, link. Have phone and laptop charged.
- Plan to join 5 minutes early. If phone interview, have notes visible but not full script.
4) During the interview
- Start by breathing for 3 slow breaths. Pause before answering to collect your structure.
- Use STAR for behavioral questions (Situation, Task, Action, Result). Be specific with numbers when you can.
- If you don’t know, say “I don’t have that experience yet, but I would…” and outline a concrete approach.
- Keep answers 1–2 minutes. Ask a thoughtful question at the end (team size, first 3 months’ goals).

5) After — quick win
- Send a 1–2 sentence thank-you note repeating one point you enjoyed and why you fit.

Do it promptly, politely, and help the relationship (not just the role). Short, specific, and grateful is best. Send a crisp email within 24–48 hours of deciding; save the wording I give you and edit only the bracketed bits. Include these elements, in this order:
1) Clear opening: say you’re declining and name the role.  
2) Gratitude: one concrete line about what you appreciated (their time, a specific conversation, something you learned).  
3) Reason: one short, non-blaming reason (keep it high-level). Avoid detailed negatives about the company, team, or process.  
4) Leave the door open: say you hope to stay in touch and mention a concrete future touchpoint if you can (connect on LinkedIn, check in in X months).  
5) Close courteously.

Tone: professional, warm, concise (3–6 short sentences). Don’t over-explain or apologize repeatedly.
